Understanding the role of motivation in engaging students with laboratory skill instruction is essential for promoting learning and academic success. Physical science laboratories function as experiential learning environments that support the development of advanced conceptual understanding; students’ attitudes toward these settings influence the effectiveness of skill acquisition. During the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as an alternative medium for skill training and experimentation that is compatible with lockdown constraints. Nevertheless, VL adoption has been limited, in part because many instructors and students lack awareness of and familiarity with these systems.

This study investigated the principal motivational factors that affect the effectiveness of VLs for teaching laboratory skills. Data were collected via a survey that combined the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) to assess intrinsic motivational components, self-reported measures addressing extrinsic influences, and a teacher perception scale regarding VLs. Data analysis employed independent-samples t-tests and automatic linear modeling to identify associations between motivational variables and performance outcomes.

Results indicate that animated graphical materials in VLs elicited stronger intrinsic motivation than e-book formats. Instructor-related variables also played a significant role in enhancing students’ motivation to engage in VL-based experiments. In addition, repeated or extended engagement with VL experiments was positively associated with improvements in laboratory performance. These findings highlight the importance of instructional design and teacher support in maximizing the motivational and pedagogical benefits of virtual laboratory environments.
